doc.title: Marty Grosz interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 4, 1995

title: Why a rhythm player: always busy hands
summary: He wonders whether rhythm guitar suited him because it let him avoid the spotlight, and likes that the hands are always occupied.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: Well you sacrifice something for it. Not that I ever had it. Some of this, you know we compensate for our shortcomings. And maybe rhythm guitar is an easy thing, it can’t be heard too well. And maybe when I was just a kid trying to get it together, it was a good instrument to be part of the group with, without ever really having to be put on the spot. That could be a thing too. I’ve thought about that as I review my life. I’ve thought about that.
Why did I pick this exact thing to do?

And then it’s also like piano in the sense that your hands are always onto something. You know the saxophone players when they’re not playing they have to stand there and either look engaged or sometimes they look disengaged. Or the trumpet players or others. But the rhythm section’s always got something under the hands. And I remember when I was a kid I used to have poison ivy a lot and stuff like that I’d be going like this. And my mother would say, “Don’t scratch, you’ll spread it.” And there’s nothing like a guitar or a piano, because it’s like scratching. You’re doing this. Something’s always happening. You’re always busy. You’re never bored. I always pitied the poor guys that have these long rests and they sit there while some guy’s taking a solo, you know.
Yeah. A lot of down time.
